summary:
We developed Junior Martian Outpost Commander, a browser-based 3D game where students plan and manage a Mars mission. Players pack limited supplies, land a spacecraft, and explore three Martian sectors while maintaining power, life support, and food production. NASA DONKI space-weather records inform storm scenarios, with simulated training drills available when needed.

The game addresses the astronaut mission trainer challenge by making engineering trade-offs part of gameplay. Carrying more shielding leaves less room for other supplies, while keeping life support running consumes power needed elsewhere. Players see the consequences of their decisions and review their choices in a mission debrief.

Our goal is to help students understand why survival beyond Earth depends on careful planning and connected systems.
details:
Junior Martian Outpost Commander is a browser-based 3D game where students manage a mission to Mars. Players begin by packing oxygen and water, solar power cells, and radiation shielding within a 1,200 kg cargo limit. They then land their spacecraft and explore three sectors: Jezero Crater, Valles Marineris, and Olympus Foothills. Each location introduces tasks such as repairing solar arrays, managing a greenhouse, drilling for ice, and producing rocket fuel from local resources. Players must complete these tasks while managing their remaining supplies and responding to emergencies.

The main benefit is that students can see the consequences of their decisions. Packing more shielding leaves less room for other supplies. During a resupply delay, keeping life support running uses power that might also be needed for other equipment. These situations give students a reason to think about priorities and explain their choices. A mission debrief brings those decisions together so players can review what happened and consider a different approach on their next attempt.

Our intended impact is to help young learners understand why surviving on another planet requires careful planning. We want players to recognise that power, water, food production, and crew safety depend on each other. The game is intended for independent exploration and could also support classroom discussions about space science and resource management. Cadet mode targets ages 7–10, while Commander mode provides more demanding challenges for players aged 11 and above.

We developed the core game using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Babylon.js handles the 3D environment, and Vite supports development and builds. We also used GPT Astra and Google AI Studio to assist with the development of the project. The source code is available on GitHub, and the playable website is hosted on Vercel. Players can access the game through a browser without installing a separate application or using specialist hardware.

The game also requests recent space-weather records from NASA’s DONKI database to inform its solar-storm scenarios. It can provide a labelled training drill when the data is unavailable or conditions are calm. Mars mission references provide context for activities such as ice extraction, communication, and local resource use. The game simplifies these concepts for learning; its resource percentages, radiation effects, and scoring are gameplay models rather than real mission predictions.

The creative element is how the science becomes part of the player’s responsibilities. Students adjust solar equipment because their outpost needs power. They manage greenhouse resources because food production competes with other needs. The fuel-production task introduces in-situ resource utilization, or ISRU, by asking players to use resources available on Mars to prepare for escape. Exploration and puzzles give these concepts a purpose within the mission.

Our main design considerations were the players’ ages, the balance between scientific detail and playability, and ease of access. The two difficulty modes change actual gameplay requirements, including solar-panel alignment tolerance and the timing window for ice drilling. Tasks become available progressively so players encounter new challenges as they advance. Browser access makes the prototype easier to share, while the training-drill fallback allows the storm activity to continue if the NASA data request fails. We also distinguish retrieved data from simplified game rules so players can understand which parts represent scientific information and which parts support the learning experience.

Playable game: https://teamcgi.vercel.app/

Source code: https://github.com/Muhammad-Khizer-Wajid/ares-outpost
